ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Polycarbonate (PC), a widely used thermoplastic, poses significant environmental challenges due to its persistence and the release of bisphenol A (BPA), a known xenoestrogen. Here, we report the isolation of Bacillus subtilis JNU01 (BsJNU01), capable of utilizing PC as its sole carbon source. Through transcriptomic analysis, we identified metallophosphoesterase from BsJNU01 (BsMPPE), the first reported metallophosphoesterase capable of degrading polycarbonate by catalyzing the hydrolysis of carbonate ester bonds. This enzyme operates under mild aqueous conditions (30 °C, pH 7), releasing 30 μmol of BPA as a monomer and demonstrating effective PC degradation under environmentally friendly conditions. PC biodegradation was confirmed by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). Furthermore, surface and mechanical analyses revealed significant degradation and structural changes in PC films following BsMPPE treatment, with toughness showing a 40–70 % decrease compared to untreated PC films. This study represents a breakthrough in microbial plastic degradation, establishing a sustainable biocatalytic platform for PC recycling and upcycling technologies.

ce:section.ce:para: In contemporary society, the versatility of plastics has provided numerous benefits to various industries; however, it has also led to significant environmental challenges [1,2]. Bisphenol A (BPA)-based polycarbonate (PC), a widely utilized polymer, is synthesized through the reaction of the petroleum-derived compound, BPA, and phosgene [3]. Owing to its outstanding characteristics, such as heat resistance, durability, and optical transparency, PC finds applications in diverse fields, including electronics, automotive components, medical devices, eyewear lenses, and packaging, with annual production exceeding 5 million tons since its invention in the 1950s [2,4]. However, environmental exposure leads to the natural degradation of PC over time, resulting in the persistent release of BPA, which is recognized as a xenoestrogen with estrogen-like properties [5,6].

To address PC waste management challenges, various mechanical and chemical degrading processes have been explored [7–12]. Mechanical recycling often results in reduced material quality and generates microplastics without eliminating the environmental impact of chemical components [13]. Chemical degradation processes are associated with high costs and energy consumption, along with increased chemical consumption and waste production, thereby amplifying their environmental footprint [4]. Current disposal methods, including landfills, incineration, and chemical treatment, are insufficient for managing the large quantity of plastic waste. These limitations highlight the urgent need for alternative recycling routes. Therefore, alternative recycling routes, such as biological degradation, should be explored [14]. Eco-friendly biological approaches offer a sustainable solution by efficiently degrading plastics under mild conditions and converting them into value-added bio-products.

Recent studies have investigated microbial biodegradation of PC waste, identifying bacterial strains such as Bacillus cereus, Bacillus megaterium, and Pseudomonas sp. NYZ600 capable of degrading PC [15–17]. However, these studies primarily demonstrate surface corrosion effects without identifying specific biocatalysts for efficient PC degradation. Notably, commercial lipases from Novozymes (Copenhagen, Denmark) have been experimentally shown to catalyze PC degradation in organic solvents, but remain constrained by insufficient data and a lack of evidence for practical biodegradation under environmentally relevant conditions [18,19]. Therefore, identifying biocatalysts from microorganisms that can effectively degrade PC under mild aqueous conditions remains a significant challenge. Furthermore, effective biocatalysts could facilitate the production of BPA as a monomer from PC waste for resynthesis or conversion into bio-products via metabolic pathways.

In this study, Bacillus subtilis JNU01 (BsJNU01), a PC-degrading bacterium, was successfully isolated from a landfill site. To identify the enzymatic mechanism underlying PC degradation, we investigated its biochemical and structural properties. Through transcriptomic analysis, we discovered a novel extracellular esterase, BsMPPE, which catalyzes the hydrolysis of PC under aqueous conditions. Our newly discovered esterase efficiently hydrolyzes PC under mild, neutral aqueous conditions without requiring organic solvents or extreme reaction conditions, highlighting its enhanced environmental applicability and potential for sustainable PC biodegradation technologies. Further biochemical characterization confirmed its role in PC degradation, establishing BsMPPE as an effective biocatalyst for sustainable plastic recycling. These findings provide a foundation for developing efficient biotechnological approaches for polycarbonate biodegradation and upcycling.

Luria–Bertani (LB) broth low salt (10.0 g/l tryptone, 5.0 g/l yeast extract, and 5.0 g/l NaCl), M9 minimal broth (6.0 g/l Na2HPO4, 3.0 g/l KH2PO4, 0.5 g/l NaCl, and 1.0 g/l NH4Cl), and a 0.1 % (v/v) trace element solution (21.8 mg/l CoCl2·6 H2O, 21.6 mg/l NiCl2·6 H2O, 24.6 mg/l CuSO4·5 H2O, 1.62 g/l FeCl3·6 H2O, 0.78 g/l CaCl2, and 14.7 mg/l MnCl2·4 H2O) were prepared for the study. Methanol and chloroform were purchased from Duksan Chemicals (Ansan, Republic of Korea). The PC was supplied by Lotte Chemical (Daejeon, Republic of Korea), and BSTFA-TMCS (99:1) was acquired from Tokyo Chemical Industry (TCI, Tokyo, Japan).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Prepartion of PC powder and film
ce:section.ce:para: The PC powder was dissolved in chloroform to form a solution with a concentration of approximately 2.5 wt%. This PC solution was then precipitated in methanol to increase the external surface area of the PC powder. The precipitated PC product was filtered using vacuum filtration. The resultant PC product was thoroughly washed several times with fresh methanol and then dried in a dispersed state—first in an oven at 50 °C for 24 h and then in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 24 h—to prevent agglomeration. To prepare the PC film, PC powder was dissolved in chloroform at a concentration of 5 % (w/v) under continuous stirring at room temperature until a homogeneous solution was obtained. The fully dissolved PC solution was poured onto a clean glass Petri dish covered with a thin layer of aluminum foil. The aluminum foil was perforated with several small holes to regulate the solvent evaporation rate, preventing the formation of bubbles or irregular thickness. After casting, the solvent was allowed to evaporate slowly in a well-ventilated environment to prevent rapid shrinkage and internal stress development within the film. Once most of the solvent had evaporated, the PC film was carefully detached from the glass Petri dish and subjected to preliminary drying in an oven set at 50 °C. This step ensured the removal of the majority of residual solvent. To further enhance the mechanical properties and achieve complete solvent removal, the sample was subsequently dried in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for several hours. The final PC film was stored in a desiccator to prevent moisture absorption and contamination before further analysis or application.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Screening and identification of PC-degradable bacteria
ce:section.ce:para: The BsJNU01 strain used in this study was isolated from soil collected at the Gwangju landfill [20]. The soil sample was processed using phosphate-buffered saline, filtered (11 μm pore size), and inoculated onto an M9MB agar plate containing 1 g/l PC. After a 7-day incubation at 28 °C, colonies were purified through repeated streaking. Microbial identification was conducted via 16S rRNA sequencing (27 F/1492 R primers, Solgent, Daejeon, Republic of Korea). BsJNU01 was cultured overnight in LB broth at 28 °C with shaking at 200 rpm. Afterward, the culture was centrifuged at 24 °C and 13,000 rpm for 20 min, and the resulting cell pellet was washed twice with M9MB media to remove any residual carbon source. PC powder at concentrations of 4 and 6 mg/ml was added in 125 ml flasks, and BsJNU01 was inoculated to achieve an OD600 of 0.2. The cultures were then incubated at 28 °C with shaking at 200 rpm for 14 days, with OD measurements taken at 2-day intervals.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Physicochemical analysis of PC degradation by BsJNU01
ce:section.ce:para: FT-IR spectroscopy was conducted using a Spectrum 100 FT-IR spectrometer (PerkinElmer, USA), with a resolution of 4 cm−1 in a wavenumber range of 4000–500 cm−1. 1H NMR spectra were obtained at the Korea Basic Science Institute (KBSI, Gwangju, Republic of Korea) using a nuclear magnetic resonance spectrometer (AscendTM 400 instrument, 400 MHz, Bruker, USA). The PC polymer solution for 1H NMR spectroscopy was prepared at a concentration of 0.5 wt% using CDCl3 (chloroform-d) as the solvent. Chemical shifts were recorded in parts per million (ppm), with residual peaks at 7.27 ppm for CDCl3 and 1.56 ppm for H2O. XPS analysis was performed using an XPS instrument (Thermofisher Scientific, K-Alpha+, USA) at the Chonnam Research Facility Center (CCRF, Gwangju, Republic of Korea). For XPS analysis, PC powder was dried in a vacuum oven at 80 °C for 24 h.

To estimate the hydrophobicity/hydrophilicity of the film surface, the average water contact angle of the PC film was measured using a contact angle analyzer (Phoenix 300, SEO, Republic of Korea) equipped with an angle meter. SEM measurement was conducted using an SEM (JSM-7900F, JEOL, Japan) at the Chonnam National University Engineering Practice Education Center (Gwangju, Republic of Korea). For SEM measurement, the surface of the film sample was coated with Pt for 40 seconds to create an electron path, preventing surface charging. The glass transition temperatures of the PC samples were measured using a DSC3 instrument (Mettler Toledo, Switzerland). Measurements were taken from 25 °C to 300 °C for the first sequence, followed by cooling to 25 °C and reheating to 300 °C in a nitrogen atmosphere with a scanning rate of 10 °C/min for the second sequence. The mechanical properties of the PC films, measuring 1 cm in width and 2 cm in length, were measured using a UTM (force tester MCT-2150, A&D, Japan) at a stretching speed of 1 mm/min. PC incubated in pure culture medium for 14 days was used as a control to ensure that the observed physicochemical changes were solely attributable to BsJNU01, rather than the medium itself.

ce:section.ce:section-title: GC-MS analysis of BsJNU01-based PC degradation products
ce:section.ce:para: GC-MS analysis was performed using a Shimadzu-QP2020 NX instrument (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan) equipped with a DB-5ms column (Agilent, Santa Clara). Subsequently, 1 µL of the sample was injected into the GC-MS in splitless mode. For the bacterial culture medium, helium was used as the carrier gas at a flow rate of 27.4 ml/min. The column temperature was initially set at 40 °C and maintained for 2 min, then ramped up at a rate of 6 °C/min until reaching 290 °C and held for 3 min. The ion source and interface temperatures were set at 200 °C and 260 °C, respectively. The GC-MS data acquisition mode was set to scan, capturing full scan spectra in the range of 30–600 m/z.

BsJNU01 was cultured in M9MB medium with PC as the sole carbon source at 28 °C and 280 rpm for three days. Control cultures lacking PC were prepared in parallel, with all experiments were performed in biological triplicates. Total RNA was isolated from bacterial cultures using Monarch® Total RNA Miniprep Kit (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, UK). The quality and quantity of isolated RNA were assessed using both a Bioanalyzer 2100 system (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, USA) and Nanodrop ND-2000 Spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, USA). Following ribosomal RNA depletion using NEBNext rRNA Depletion kit (New England Biolabs), RNA libraries were constructed using TruSeq Stranded Total RNA Library Prep Kit with Ribo-Zero Gold (Illumina, San Diego, USA). Library quality was verified using TapeStation HS D1000 Screen Tape (Agilent Technologies), and quantification was performed using a StepOne Real-Time PCR System (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, USA). The prepared libraries were then sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform using paired-end 151 bp reads.

Raw sequence reads were quality-filtered and trimmed for adapter sequences using Trimmomatic (v0.39) [21]. The reference genome and annotation files of B. subtilis HY2–62 (GCF_029542145.1) were obtained from the NCBI database. A genome index was constructed using Bowtie2 (v2.4.5) [22], and the cleaned reads were aligned to this index using default parameters. The resulting alignment files were processed with StringTie (v2.2.1) and prepDE [23] to quantify transcript abundances, expressed as both transcripts per kilobase million (TPM) and counts per million mapped reads (CPM). Differential expression analysis was performed using edgeR (v3.38.4) [24], with genes considered differentially expressed if they met the following criteria: read count > 10 in at least one sample, false discovery rate (q-value) < 0.01, and absolute log2 fold change > 1. The protein sequence features of the LFL98_RS11595 were analyzed using InterProScan (v98.0) [25], with results visualized in R software.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Cloning, overexpression, and purification of the esterase from BsJNU01
ce:section.ce:para: Genomic DNA extracted from BsJNU01 was used to encode the esterase gene. The primer sequences utilized for esterase gene cloning are provided (Table S5). The DNA fragments, amplified through PCR, were purified using the Wizard® SV Gel and PCR Clean-Up System (Promega, Madison, WI, USA) and subsequently ligated into the pET28a(+) vector or pLIC.B4 vector (including His6, MBP, and TEV protease cleavage site at the N-terminus) using the Gibson Assembly® Master Mix (New England Biolabs). For cloning and expression, the broth and agar contained 30 µg/ml kanamycin for the pET28a vector and 50 µg/ml ampicillin for the pLIC.B4 vector. The cloned DNA in pET28a(+) or pLIC.B4 was transformed into the E. coli C2566 strain using an electroporator (MicroPulser, Bio-Rad, Hercules, USA) and then spread on LB agar. DNA sequencing was conducted using Sanger sequencing (Macrogen, Daejeon, Republic of Korea). The transformants were then plated on LB agar and cultured overnight at 37 °C.

Subsequently, they were inoculated into 10 ml of LB broth, and a 1 % aliquot of the cell culture was inoculated into a 500 ml LB medium. The cells were grown under conditions of 37 °C and 200 rpm, reaching an OD600 of approximately 0.6–0.8. Then, 0.1 mM isopropyl-β-d-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) was added, and the culture was incubated at 20 °C with shaking at 150 rpm for 16 h. The E. coli cells containing the overexpressed esterases were harvested by centrifugation at 4000 rpm for 20 min at 4 °C and then stored at −80 °C.

The cell pellet was resuspended in an ice-cold lysis buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) and 500 mM NaCl, then disrupted by ultrasonication (Fisher Scientific, Pittsburgh, PA). The supernatant was collected by centrifugation at 13,000 rpm for 20 min at 4 °C and loaded onto a Ni-charged immobilized metal ion affinity chromatography column (ELPIS, Daejeon, Republic of Korea). The bound proteins were eluted with varying concentrations of imidazole in the lysis buffer, up to a maximum of 250 mM. The purified enzyme was then desalted using a 30 kDa or 50 kDa molecular weight cutoff ultracentrifugal filtration tube (Amicon, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, USA) and dialyzed against 100 mM potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7.5). Gene expression was assessed through both SDS-PAGE and enzyme activity assays.

The enzyme activity was assessed using a reaction mixture containing 50 mM CHES buffer (pH 9.0), 1 mM p-nitrophenyl esters (C8–C14), and 1 μM BsMPPE at 30 °C. Reactions were terminated by adding 2 M sodium carbonate and 5 μl Triton X-100. The release of p-nitrophenol was determined spectrophotometrically by measuring absorbance at 415 nm, with product quantification achieved using a standard curve generated with known concentrations of p-nitrophenol. Control reactions without the enzyme were conducted to eliminate background hydrolysis of the p-nitrophenyl esters. Additionally, BsMPPE was treated with 0–0.5 mM MnCl2 or ZnCl2 for 30 min at 30 °C, followed by pNP assay.

The degradation reaction of PC by esterase was performed in 100 mM potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) containing 6 mg/ml PC powder and 0.4 mg/ml esterase for 24 h. After the reactions had been quenched by adding 3 ml of ethyl acetate (EA), 50 μl of 10 mM tridecanoic acid was added as an internal standard. The mixture was vigorously vortexed for 5 min and then centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 10 min to ensure thorough extraction. The organic phase was extracted and evaporated using SpeedVac. Subsequently, the degradation products were resuspended in EA. The resolved products were treated with silylation using BSTFA-TMCS in a 1:1 ratio, and the reaction was conducted at 70 °C for 30 min. For the analysis of BsMPPE-catalyzed PC hydrolysis, helium served as the carrier gas at a flow rate of 27.4 ml/min. The column temperature was initially set at 70 °C and maintained for 2 min, then ramped up at a rate of 5 °C/min to reach 130 °C in the first stage, followed by a second ramp at a rate of 10 °C/min to reach 180 °C. The final stage involved a ramp at a rate of 5 °C/min to reach 285 °C, which was maintained for 1 min. The ion source and interface temperatures were set at 230 °C and 290 °C, respectively. The GC-MS data acquisition mode was configured for scanning, capturing full scan spectra in the range of 33–750 m/z.

The BsJNU01 strain for PC biodegradation was isolated from soil samples collected 11 m below the surface at the Gwangju landfill [20]. Furthermore, we found that this strain could thrive exclusively in M9 minimal broth (M9MB), using PC powder as the sole carbon source. Based on the maximum-likelihood phylogenetic analysis of 16S rRNA sequences, BsJNU01 was confirmed to belong to the Bacillus subtilis species, forming a distinct and well-supported clade within the B. subtilis group with bootstrap values greater than 90 % ( Fig. 1A and Table S1). To characterize the growth of this newly identified strain, PC concentrations were set at 4 mg/ml and 6 mg/ml, with bacterial growth monitored by measuring the optical density at 600 nm (OD600) for 14 days at 2-day intervals. At both concentrations, BsJNU01 showed a notable increase in OD600, reaching the stationary phase within two days (Fig. 1B). Maximum OD600 values of 0.57 and 1.33 were achieved at concentrations of 4 mg/ml and 6 mg/ml over four days, respectively. In the control medium containing only plastic, OD600 remained constant, confirming contamination in the culture environment. When only microorganisms were present, OD600 decreased, indicating the absence of a carbon source. However, media supplemented with both plastic and microorganisms showed a marked increase in OD600, indicating the ability to use plastic as the sole carbon source.

We demonstrated BsJNU01 strain-induced PC biodegradation, confirming modifications in the chemical structure. PC, which contains hydrolyzable carbonate bonds, typically undergoes hydrolytic-type decomposition. Specifically, the carbonyl carbon atom of the PC chain is electrophilic, making it more susceptible to attack by hydroxide ions under basic conditions. This leads to terminal cleavage of the PC chain, releasing CO2 and hydroxyl groups [15]. Recent studies on PC biodegradation further suggest that, due to the bond dissociation energy of PC model compounds, the bond within the carbonate’s O-CO group the second weakest linkage in the structure is likely to be cleaved by hydrolytic enzymes ( Fig. 2A) [15]. FT-IR spectroscopy was performed to analyze the chemical structural changes in the PC sample following biodegradation by BsJNU01 (Fig. 2B-C). PC incubated in pure culture medium for 14 days was used as a control to confirm that the observed changes were induced solely by the BsJNU01 strain, ensuring that the physicochemical modifications were unrelated to the medium itself. The FT-IR spectra of the pure PC and biodegraded PC display characteristic peaks, such as C-O-C and CO bonds. Specifically, the peak intensity of the C-H vibration mode, corresponding to the aromatic ring, appeared in the 2870–3000 cm−1 range [26]. Fig. 2C presents the enlarged FT-IR spectra for the pure PC and the biodegraded PC by BsJNU01, highlighting the C-O-C stretching vibration mode at 1180–1222 cm−1 range, as well as the CO stretching vibration mode at 1766 cm−1 [27]. The peak intensities of the C-O-C and CO bonds decreased in the biodegraded sample compared with the control sample, possibly indicating cleavage of the carbonate bond in PC [26]. In contrast, the peak intensity of the hydroxyl group (-OH) significantly increased from 3200 cm−1 to 3600 cm−1, which may be attributed to the presence of hydroxyl groups at both terminal sites of the biodegraded PC [16]. These results indirectly suggest the PC biodegradation, however, additional analyses are required to precisely interpret the chemical structural modifications observed in the FT-IR spectra.

The 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) spectra of the pure PC and biodegraded PC matched the FT-IR results, supporting the cleavage of the PC backbone into BPA (Fig. 2D). The peaks at δ = 7.07–7.19 ppm correspond to the protons for the benzene ring (designated as “a” and “b”), while the peaks at δ = 1.62 ppm correspond to the protons for the methyl groups (designated as “c”). Comparison of the spectra revealed no peak change (e.g., peak shift or peak disappearance) between the pure PC and biodegraded PC [28–30]. This finding indicates that the benzene ring and methyl groups of PC are preserved after biodegradation by BsJNU01. Given the identical chemical structure of the BPA for benzene ring and methyl groups, it is evident that cleavage of the PC backbone occurs at the carbonate bond. The 1H NMR spectrum of the biodegraded PC by the BsJNU01 strain revealed a new peak at δ = 4.74 ppm, corresponding to the hydroxyl group (-OH) of the biodegraded PC (Fig. 2E) [30]. This result suggests that the PC was successfully degraded by the BsJNU01 strain via cleavage of the carbonate bond, thereby forming BPA.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) results for pure PC and biodegraded PC by BsJNU01 (Fig. S1). The XPS full spectra covering the entire binding energy range from 1300 to 0 eV for these samples are displayed in Fig. S1A. Fig. S1B-D present the high-resolution XPS spectra of the C, O, and N elements for the pure PC and biodegraded PC by BsJNU01. All XPS spectra were normalized to facilitate comparison of peak modifications (e.g., intensity change or peak shift). The XPS spectrum of the biodegraded PC by BsJNU01 shows a decreased intensity for the C1s peak, along with a reduced intensity and peak shift for the O1s peak, indicating carbonate bond cleavage. Additionally, the XPS spectrum of the biodegraded PC by BsJNU01 reveals a new N1s peak, which is absent in the XPS spectrum of the pure PC. To further understand PC biodegradation by the BsJNU01 strain, we decoupled the C1s and O1s peaks into specific deconvolution peaks related to each chemical bond (Fig. S2). In the deconvoluted C1s peaks, the carbonate peak shifts from 289.7 eV to 289.5 eV after PC biodegradation by the BsJNU01 strain, which indicates the modification of the carbonate group, possibly due to the carbonate bond cleavage (Fig. S2A-B) [31–33]. Furthermore, the peak at 287.6 eV appears due to the formation of the OC-N bond in the biodegraded PC, which aligns with the new N1s peak [31]. As for the O1s deconvoluted peaks, the XPS spectra of pure PC and biodegraded PC by BsJNU01 exhibit two prominent peaks at 532.7 eV and 530.1 eV, corresponding to the C-O and CO bonds, respectively (Fig. S2C-D) [34–36]. Notably, the O1s XPS spectrum of the biodegraded PC by BsJNU01 strain shows a new peak at 535.1 eV, attributed to the hydroxyl group (-OH) at the terminal sites of the biodegraded PC [35]. This result indicates that biodegradation of the PC leads to the formation of BPA, with the terminal sites of the biodegraded PC featuring hydroxyl groups after the carbonate group cleavage.

The PC film was examined to assess its physical properties before and after biodegradation by the BsJNU01 strain. The biodegradation process involved treating the PC film with the BsJNU01 strain for 14 days, with an untreated pure PC film prepared for accurate comparison. A control experiment involving PC film incubated in pure culture medium for 14 days without the BsJNU01 strain was conducted to ensure that the physicochemical modifications observed were exclusively due to the enzymatic activity of BsJNU01 and not related to the culture medium itself. Fig. 3A shows the top-view SEM images for the pure PC film (control) and biodegraded PC film by BsJNU01. The pure PC film exhibited a smooth, uniform surface without noticeable cracks or pores. In contrast, the biodegraded PC film treated with BsJNU01 displayed noticeable pores (approximately 100–200 nm) on its surface (Fig. 3A). Moreover, the surface texture became rough with differences in height. These modifications in surface morphology suggest that biodegradation of the PC film by BsJNU01 may involve partial cleavage of the carbonate group in the PC backbone.

The average water contact angle was measured to assess the surface hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity of the pure and biodegraded PC films. The pure PC film exhibited an average water contact angle of 38.69°. This value indicates a relatively hydrophilic nature due to oxygen-rich sites, in contrast to other commercial hydrocarbon polymers, such as polyethylene (PE) and polystyrene (PS) [20,37]. Conversely, the biodegraded PC film showed a significantly higher average water contact angle of 53.87°, suggesting a shift toward hydrophobicity (Fig. 3B). This increased average water contact angle value may be attributed to the oxygen deficiency in the biodegraded PC backbone with carbonate group cleavage. Additionally, SEM images confirmed that the biodegraded PC film by BsJNU01 had a rougher surface, likely contributing to lower water wettability, consistent with the Wenzel or Cassie–Baxter models [37–40].

The PC film degraded by BsJNU01 exhibited a significant reduction in mechanical properties, as evidenced by a decrease in the maximum tensile strength from 86 MPa in the control sample to 80 MPa. The stress–strain curve showed a notable reduction in elongation at break, which dropped from 91 % to 55 %, indicating the film’s diminished ability to withstand deformation before failure. Young’s modulus also decreased substantially, from 430 MPa to 180 MPa, and the toughness was nearly halved, decreasing from 72 J/cm³ to 38 J/cm³ . Additionally, thermal analysis via differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) revealed a reduction in the glass transition temperature (Tg) from 143 °C in the untreated film to 139 °C and 136 °C in the BsJNU01-treated samples, indicating a loss in thermal stability (Table S2, Fig. S3).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Identification and analysis of the by-products after BsJNU01 treatment
ce:section.ce:para: GC-MS analysis was performed to identify the monomers released during PC biodegradation by BsJNU01. The analysis was conducted on a bacterial culture broth containing PC as the sole carbon source for eight days. The bacterial culture broth was extracted with dichloromethane to isolate PC degradation products. As a result, BPA was detected as a released metabolite in the BsJNU01-treated PC culture solution (Fig. 3C). The detection of BPA as a monomer of PC is particularly significant, as it directly indicates the cleavage of carbonate bonds within the PC polymer chains [16,18,19,38]. This finding suggests that the BsJNU01 strain can effectively depolymerize PC into BPA as its constituent monomers and smaller compounds. Furthermore, comparisons with existing studies enhance the understanding of microbial PC degradation, as it has been demonstrated that P. sp. NyZ600 degrades PC, thereby producing BPA and other byproducts [16]. The similarities in degradation products suggest that BsJNU01 may employ similar enzymatic pathways or mechanisms. To confirm that BPA production is enzymatically driven, we performed an additional assay using heat-inactivated enzyme. The native enzyme yielded significantly higher BPA levels compared to both the control and heat-inactivated conditions, supporting that BPA formation is dependent on enzymatic activity of BsJNU01 (Fig. S8).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Identification of a novel PC-degrading enzyme through transcriptome analysis
ce:section.ce:para: To elucidate the molecular basis of PC degradation in BsJNU01, we employed RNA sequencing to identify enzymes specifically induced during PC metabolism. Using B. subtilis HY2–62 as a reference genome (100 % 16S rRNA sequence identity with BsJNU01), we performed comparative transcriptome analysis between cells cultivated in M9 minimal medium with and without PC as the sole carbon source. RNA sequencing generated an average of 74.8 million reads per sample across biological replicates (nControl = 3, nPC = 2; Table S3). Following quality control and preprocessing, we obtained 62.0 million high-quality reads, with 61.65 % mapping uniquely to the reference genome.

Differential expression analysis identified 182 significantly regulated enzymes, with 60 showing upregulation and 122 displaying downregulation in response to PC exposure ( Fig. 4A). Given that PC degradation likely involves hydrolytic cleavage of carbonate ester bonds, we focused our analysis on enzymes encoding lipase and esterase. Our genome analysis revealed 39 potential hydrolases (5 lipases, 32 esterases, and 2 esterase/lipase family proteins; Table S4). Notably, among these candidates, only a single metallophosphoesterase (MPPE; locus tag LFL98_RS11595) exhibited significant upregulation under PC treatment conditions (Fig. 4B).

The MPPE belongs to a family of metal-dependent hydrolases that typically cleave phosphoester bonds [39], suggesting its potential to hydrolyze the structurally analogous carbonate ester linkages in PC. Protein sequence analysis revealed that LFL98_RS11595 contains membrane-associated domains, indicating optimal positioning for accessing and degrading extracellular polymeric substrates. Based on its specific induction during PC metabolism, predicted catalytic mechanism, and strategic cellular localization, we identified LFL98_RS11595 as a promising candidate for PC degradation and designated it as BsMPPE.

To confirm the activity of the BsMPPE, recombinant BsMPPE was expressed in Escherichia coli (E. coli) C2566 and purified using His-tag chromatography. Native BsMPPE exhibited a very low expression level in E. coli; therefore, the target gene was engineered to translate the protein in a fused state with a His6 tag, maltose-binding protein (MBP), and tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease cleavage site at the N-terminus to enhance solubility [40]. The molecular masses of the recombinant BsMPPE and MBP-BsMPPE were approximately 28.3 kDa and 69.7 kDa, respectively, as estimated by SDS-PAGE (Fig. S4). To verify the activity of the recombinant BsMPPE, catalytic reactions were conducted using 4-nitrophenyl esters (C8–C14), with the highest activity observed for 4-nitrophenyl octanoate (C8) (Fig. S5A). Additionally, BsMPPE functions as a metal-dependent enzyme, relying on metal ions, such as manganese and zinc, for its activity. These ions are known to facilitate substrate binding and hydrolysis reactions at the enzyme’s active site. According to the Irving–Williams series, zinc exhibits approximately twice the binding affinity of manganese. To examine whether this trend is applicable to BsMPPE, we tested the effect of Zn²⁺ on enzymatic activity. Similar to Mn²⁺, Zn²⁺ also showed maximal activity at 0.1 mM; however, the overall activity observed in the presence of Zn²⁺ was consistently lower than that of Mn²⁺ (Fig. S5B). This result suggests that while the Irving–Williams trend may be partially reflected, Mn²⁺ is more effective in enhancing BsMPPE activity under the tested conditions. The decline in activity at elevated concentrations of both metal ions may be attributed to non-specific binding or toxicity [41,42]. The presence of metal ions in BsMPPE likely provides the necessary catalytic power to break the strong ester bonds in the polymer structure of PC. The high energy requirement for cleaving these robust bonds makes BsMPPE a strong candidate for efficient polymer degradation. Additionally, the metal ions can facilitate the hydrolytic cleavage of the carbonate ester bonds, thereby promoting the breakdown of the polymer into simpler compounds.

Next, the BsMPPE enzyme reaction was performed on both PC powder and PC film to confirm the PC-hydrolyzing activity of BsMPPE. SEM analysis of the PC film treated with purified BsMPPE enzyme revealed significant changes ( Fig. 5A). The pure PC film displayed a smooth surface, whereas the BsMPPE-treated PC film exhibited a damaged and cracked surface. GC-MS analysis was conducted to identify PC degradation products in the reaction solution containing purified BsMPPE and PC. The control sample (pure PC film without BsMPPE enzyme) and the BsMPPE-treated PC powder sample were incubated at 30 °C and 200 rpm for 24 h. As a result, BPA was detected as a released monomer in the BsMPPE-treated PC powder sample (Fig. 5B).

The mechanical properties of the pure PC film and biodegraded PC film by the BsMPPE enzyme were measured using a Universal Testing Machine (UTM) (Table S2 and Fig. S6A) [43]. The biodegraded PC film by the BsMPPE enzyme exhibited a substantial reduction in tensile strength (38 MPa), elongation at break (45 %), and Young’s modulus (49 MPa) compared to those of the pure PC film (71 MPa, 74 %, and 140 MPa, respectively). Additionally, the biodegraded PC film by the BsMPPE enzyme showed a significant decrease in toughness (13 J/cm3), reflecting its diminished capacity to absorb energy during deformation. Thermal analysis of the BsMPPE-treated PC film further revealed a decrease in Tg from 140 °C in the control sample to 138 °C and 137 °C, indicating a loss in thermal stability (Fig. S6B-D).

ce:section.ce:section-title: BPA production from PC by BsMPPE
ce:section.ce:para: We monitored BPA production at various temperatures and pH levels to assess the PC-degrading activity of the selected BsMPPE (Fig. S7A-B). After optimizing pH and temperature, we confirmed that the enzyme exhibited maximum activity at 30 °C and pH 11. However, this increased activity at high pH levels is not directly attributable to the enzyme; rather, it is interpreted as a consequence of increased hydrolysis reactions with increasing pH. Previous reports have indicated that PC hydrolysis accelerates with rising pH and temperature [44]. Therefore, we conducted a time-course experiment under conditions unaffected by external influences (30 °C and pH 7). BPA production was detected (5.97 ± 0.64 μM) in the control group without enzyme activity. This occurs due to the incomplete polymerization of PC, leading to the release of BPA [45–47].

After experimentation, we confirmed that the enzyme maintains its activity for 8–48 h, during which the turbidity of the solution gradually increased due to the degradation of the PC polymer bond (Fig. 5A). Under optimized conditions, the enzyme exhibited significant catalytic activity, resulting in the effective cleavage of carbonate bonds within the PC polymer chains. This was evidenced by the production of approximately 10 µM of BPA, confirmed through GC-MS analysis (Fig. 5B). Compared to untreated films, those treated with BsMPPE exhibited significant reductions in maximum tensile strength, elongation at break, Young’s modulus, and toughness (Table S2 and Fig. S6A). The biodegradation of PC by the BsMPPE enzyme deteriorates the PC film by cleaving its carbonate group-based backbone, leading to diminished mechanical properties. These reduced mechanical properties are consistent with the porous morphologies and abundant defects observed in the SEM images (Fig. 5A).

Comparatively, the study utilizing Candida rugosa-derived lipase demonstrated a significant reduction in PC weight, achieving up to 60 % degradation within 72 h. Despite this impressive result, it is important to note that the PC used in the C. rugosa experiments was pretreated with the strong oxidizing agent, hypochlorite [19]. This pretreatment likely enhanced the substrate’s susceptibility to enzymatic degradation, thus making direct comparisons between the two studies challenging. In contrast, our study demonstrates that BsMPPE operates under mild aqueous conditions (30 °C, pH 7) without requiring harsh chemical pretreatment or organic solvents. While the calculated degradation efficiency of BsMPPE (∼0.015 %) is modest compared to systems involving chemical pretreatment, its ability to degrade PC directly under environmentally relevant conditions represents a significant step forward in developing sustainable and scalable solutions for plastic waste management. Furthermore, eliminating the use of strong oxidizing agents aligns with green chemistry principles and reduces potential environmental hazards, making BsMPPE a more eco-friendly alternative for future applications in plastic recycling technologies.

Through transcriptome analysis of wild-type bacteria, this study firstly identified a novel BsMPPE enzyme from B. subtilis JNU01, demonstrating remarkable capability in biodegrading PC, a synthetic polymer traditionally known for its resistance to degradation. The biodegradation ability of BsJNU01 was systematically validated through multiple analytical techniques, including FT-IR spectroscopy, NMR, XPS, SEM, and GC-MS analyses, which provided detailed molecular insights into the PC degradation mechanism orchestrated by this newly identified esterase. The isolated BsJNU01 strain showed remarkable potential in PC biodegradation by efficiently utilizing PC powder as its sole carbon source in M9MB medium, achieving substantial growth within two days. This rapid adaptation underscores its metabolic versatility and promising potential for large-scale bioremediation applications, offering a strategic approach to address the growing challenge of PC waste management.

Differential expression analysis revealed a key upregulated metallophosphoesterase gene (LFL98_RS11595) in BsJNU01 when exposed to PC, a marking a significant breakthrough in understanding microbial PC degradation mechanisms. The encoded BsMPPE, predicted to be membrane-bound, demonstrated strong hydrolytic activity on carbonate esters, effectively catalyzing the conversion of PC to BPA under environmentally relevant conditions. Notably, this represents the first reported enzymatic system capable of degrading insoluble PC polymer in aqueous solution at room temperature and neutral pH. The ability of BsMPPE to overcome the sterically hindered ester bond of insoluble PC within 24 hour, without requiring organic solvents or extreme conditions, establishes this enzyme as a promising candidate for eco-friendly PC recycling technologies.

In previous studies, commercial lipases, such as those from C. antarctica, C. rugosa, and porcine pancreas with 22 %, 15 %, and 16 % sequence identity, respectively, compared to that of BsMPPE, have shown PC degradation activity in an organic solvent with the pretreatment of the substrate with hypochlorite, a strong oxidizing agent [19,48]. The catalytic triad (Ser, His, and Asp/Glu) in these lipases plays a crucial role in the hydrolysis of carbonate bonds, leading to the release of BPA. This mechanism is similar to ester hydrolysis by serine proteases, where the serine residue initiates polymer breakdown through nucleophilic attack [19].

By contrast, BsMPPE operates PC biodegradation in effectively under mild, aqueous conditions. Additionally, BsMPPE’s extracellular localization, facilitated by a signal peptide and the Twin-arginine translocation (Tat) pathway, ensures accessibility of polymeric substrates. Recognized by the TatA, TatB, and TatC protein complexes, BsMPPE is translocated from the cytoplasm toward the cell wall. Upon reaching the cell wall, the signal peptide of BsMPPE is cleaved, allowing the enzyme to bind to negatively charged components of the cell wall through electrostatic interactions. This binding is expected to enable BsMPPE to recognize and degrade PC in the external environment ( Fig. 6C) [49–51].

The experimental results validate the efficacy of purified BsMPPE in degrading PC and producing BPA. Future research should explore protein engineering of BsMPPE to enhance PC degradation and upcycling of PC waste using BsMPPE-adopted engineered bacteria. Notably, the assimilating metabolic pathway of BPA in Pseudomonas putida YC-AE1 have been shown to efficiently break down BPA under various environmental conditions [52]. According to multiple studies on enzyme systems involved in BPA degradation, microorganisms degrade BPA primarily through the action of oxidative enzymes, such as cytochrome P450, laccases and peroxidases [53–63]. By combining the BPA metabolic pathways with BsMPPE, efficient polycarbonate (PC) upcycling can be achieved through the production of BPA from PC degradation, followed by its utilization as microbial biomass. This approach could make the process of converting PC into microbial biomass a viable reality. Therefore, adapting BsMPPE for PC biodegradation into various bacteria strains capable of BPA degradation facilitates the development of synthetic bacteria for PC upcycling by adopting alternative metabolic pathways for producing value-added chemicals.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates the discovery of novel BsMPPE as a highly effective biocatalyst for the degradation of PC and production of BPA under environmentally relevant conditions. By integrating the BPA metabolic pathways with BsMPPE, we propose a novel approach for efficiently upcycling PC into value-added chemicals. Future research on protein engineering of BsMPPE and the development of engineered bacteria could further enhance the degradation and upcycling of PC waste, paving the way for sustainable plastic recycling and bioconversion processes.

Plastic contamination stands as a major environmental issue which needs creative sustainable approaches to handle plastic waste management. Researchers discovered Bacillus subtilis JNU01 as a new PC-degrading bacterium which produces an extracellular metallophosphoesterase enzyme called BsMPPE that performs PC depolymerization at 30 °C and pH 7. The enzyme BsMPPE breaks down carbonate bonds in PC to produce BPA monomers while changing both mechanical strength and surface characteristics of PC. The enzymatic system BsMPPE presents a sustainable and biologically compatible solution for degradation compared to traditional systems which need harsh pretreatment or organic solvents. The integration of BPA-assimilating pathways into microbial systems could enable the upcycling of PC waste into valuable bio-products which would expand its use in circular economy systems. Future research should prioritize the optimization of BsMPPE enzymatic activity and host organism engineering for complete biodegradation as well as industrial-scale application development. BsMPPE establishes itself as a major breakthrough in microbial plastic degradation because it functions as a green biocatalyst to manage polycarbonate waste responsibly. The research demonstrates how microbial solutions can solve worldwide plastic pollution problems while developing sustainable recycling and upcycling technologies.

Polycarbonate (PC) waste contributes to microplastic pollution and bisphenol A (BPA) release, posing environmental and health risks. Conventional disposal methods often exacerbate contamination, necessitating sustainable alternatives. Microbial degradation by bacteria and their enzymes offers an eco-friendly solution, reducing plastic waste and facilitating BPA recovery for reuse or conversion. Advancing these biodegradation strategies can enhance plastic waste management, mitigate ecological risks, and support a circular economy.
